chapters.html:
It has been three months since the end of the world—and forty-two days since Mydei and Phainon have spoken to each other.

To a certain degree, Mydei can’t blame him. The fight with Irontomb was brutal—entire swaths of the new planet are practically inhospitable in the wake of a Lord Ravager’s destruction. The first order of business was reestablishing farms and wells—a mission that needed all hands on deck.

They aren’t alone, at least. The Interastral Peace Corporation has offered their assistance—something Aglaea had little choice but to accept in light of the desolation. But even with resources from beyond the sky, progress is slow. Not to mention that many were reluctant to trust people from beyond the sky at all. The Chrysos Heirs may no longer have the power of simulated Titans, but their strength is still evident—as is the social capital they hold with their people.

So it makes sense, in some ways, that Phainon and Mydei have not had time to talk as in-depth as Mydei might want them to. Mydei, after all, has spent most of the last three months in Castrum Kremnos.

But that was then. This is now.

Three months after the battle with Irontomb, citizens from all over Amphoreus have returned to Okhema to celebrate the Festival of Phagousa—a way to celebrate their triumph over Irontomb and the progress of their rebuilding. Mydei himself traveled with a contingent from Castrum Kremnos at Aglaea’s request—she wanted to demonstrate the unity of the Chrysos Heirs even now. A feast is a perfect way to do it. Not that Mydei is against the idea—but it definitely wasn’t easy to pry himself away from Castrum Kremnos for the three-week festival.

Mydei has been in Okhema for fifteen days. Phainon has been in Okhema for thirteen. And they have not spoken once. Nothing more than a nod in passing. Yes, they’ve been busy—plenty of work still needs to get done. But despite their packed schedules, Mydei has still managed to have conversations with all of the other Heirs.

Hyacine sat him down for an extensive check-up, giving him advice on how to maintain his newly-mortal body. He and Anaxagoras had a brief—slightly uncomfortable—conversation about how the lack of demigodhood has affected Mydei.

Castorice—still delighted in her ability to approach the living—invited him to accompany her to one of the festival’s midnight dances. Though Mydei was hardly one to engage in such things, he did enjoy sampling street foods from the stalls set up around Mamoreal Market. And, of course, he couldn’t help but smile at the sheer elation in Castorice’s eyes when she was invited to dance by Cipher. Cipher herself approached Mydei after the festivities to… well, Mydei wasn’t exactly sure. Mostly, she made fun of his new hairstyle—apparently, his high ponytail doesn’t suit him—and then took his skewer of souvlaki

Aglaea invited him to the baths for a conversation about the rebuilding of Castrum Kremnos that, at some point, shifted into how he was faring. Mydei left the meeting with an intricately embroidered chlamys and a head bursting with advice for running a nation—many of them tips that Aglaea had learned herself in the last few months without her golden threads.

Getting to know Lady Tribios was a surreal affair. Mydei is still not quite sure about the intricate details of what Caelus, Cyrene, and the members of the so-called “Genius Society” had done to reforge Okhema and insert it into reality. Cyrene described it as “rewinding the clock.” Caelus said that they “did a Windows shutdown to make the Heirs respawn and normalify.” In the end, though, the details don’t matter. The Titans have no place in reality—and neither do the Chrysos Heirs. The curse of golden blood has been revoked, leaving Mydei mortal, Aglaea threadless, and the Ladies Tribios one.

The original Lady Tribios is just as kind and welcoming as the trio who bore her name. Though they haven’t spoken much since her body and mind was reforged, she practically leapt upon him when he returned to Okhema, demanding to know all about life in the rebuilt Castrum Kremnos.

After listening intently to Mydei’s report, Tribios pressed a handful of papers into his hands. A glance down revealed the faces of the other Chrysos Heirs beaming up at him in charcoal and watercolor. So he would have something to remind him of Okhema, Lady Tribios had said, in an action so like much Trianne it made Mydei’s heart seize.

She might not be the triplets, Tribios had said, but she had their memories. Though, she assured him, she understood if it was odd for him. She understood that he was still surely mourning Trinnon, Trianne, and Tribbie, even if they hadn’t truly vanished. That he likely didn’t know what to say to her anymore.

She was right, in her own way—he hadn’t known how to interact with her. In some ways, he still doesn’t. But the awkwardness has begun to abate. When he brings her honeycakes, she ruffles his hair and calls him “Little ‘Dei” like her segments once did.

Mydei has even interacted with Hysilens, Cerydra, and Cyrene. Apparently, he knew them in previous cycles—though none of them remember that. Still, he’s grown to appreciate all three as allies.

He particularly appreciates Hysilens’ and Cyrene’s steadfast loyalty and seemingly endless patience. Hysilens in particular has proven to be a great help in keeping morale high, and Mydei was more than willing to help her set up for Phagousa’s festival in return. Cyrene… confuses him, to be honest. Still, she’s sweet—and she seems oddly invested in making sure that Mydei is doing well. She even attempted to get Mydei to speak to Phainon once—an attempt that failed spectacularly. Not that he told her that.

Cerydra, on the other hand… she harbors a much larger personality, to put it very kindly. She’s a power-hungry woman—though she at least seems to truly want the best for Amphoreus. She had initially demanded control of Okhema from Aglaea—though that, obviously, didn’t happen. To Mydei’s understanding, she eventually took up a position as one of Aglaea’s advisors and negotiator with the IPC—a turn of events he still isn’t quite sure about.

The fact that Mydei has even managed to connect with women who had been dead before his birth makes Phainon’s absence feel that much more pronounced. In the moments where they do speak, it is just basic pleasantries—hello, good to see you, I’ve got to meet Aglaea, see you later.

To say it’s jarring would be an understatement. There was a time when they spent nearly every waking moment at each others’ side. They shared everything—breakfasts, baths, beds. There was a time where Mydei was positive Phainon was his soulmate—a concept he had found laughable at best until he met the man he considered his equal in everything, from the battlefield to the bedroom. There was even a time—admittedly only a day—where Mydei and Phainon had considered each other lovers. Proper lovers, not just bedmates. Lovers who—in that short time—stole kisses and clothing and sweet little nothings that made Mydei feel like both a fool and a man on top of the world.

When their time together ended, Mydei took a little token with him. One of Phainon’s chokers—a stupid strip of leather that had always made Mydei’s heart skip. Phainon’s choker pressed on his windpipe like a caress—just tight enough to keep him present when his mind hummed with the madness of the black tide.

He wasn’t under any sort of delusion—it was stupid. He’d been stupid. An impulsive, adrenaline-fueled declaration of love is not a promise of a life together. And Mydei, foolishly, had let himself believe it was. In the haze of battle, he replayed the memory of Phainon saying he loved Mydei, that he yearned for them to be together. Properly together. They talked about exploring their homes, lazing in golden wheatfields and exploring tranquil libraries. Splattered with golden blood, choking on his own viscera, he imagined it. When he blinked through the stinging waters of the Sea of Souls, he wondered how Phainon was doing.

Mydei isn’t a lovestruck teenager. He didn’t expect Phainon to burst from Irontomb spilling declarations of love and promises of forever. It would be impossible to go through something like that without scars—both mental and physical. He had been prepared for that. He had even been prepared for Phainon to steer clear of him for a bit—he’s always needed time on his own to process certain things. A few days. A week, perhaps. It’s happened before. But even then—he would still speak to Mydei.

He certainly didn’t expect to be ignored completely. Nothing more than strained greetings and subdued banter. Phainon didn’t even tell Mydei what he’d been through—Mydei had to piece it together himself. It’s a jab through the gut, given that Phainon once said Mydei knew him better than anyone else. And the salt in the wound—Mydei is probably the person who understands what Phainon has been through best.

Mydei’s hundreds of years have, at times, been agonizing. When the Flame Reaver plunged his scythe through his chest, his first emotion was shock. The second was grief. The third was relief. Relief at the end to his ceaseless strife. Even he can hardly imagine the agony inherent in living millions of years. Perhaps billions—Caelus had only mentioned that the total number of cycles was well over a million. He can’t blame Phainon for struggling to adjust to a reality without the cycles—to a life that’s no longer an endless battle. If he’s being honest, he struggles with that too.

What he can blame Phainon for, though, is his cowardice. At a certain point, Mydei couldn’t help but wonder if the real reason Phainon wouldn’t speak to Mydei was because he didn’t want him anymore. That would be—it would be fine. Fine. Phainon has experienced millions of lives now—it would hardly be a shock if he realized he deserved better.

That would be fine. Mydei is a warrior; he’s handled far worse than the love of his life telling him he doesn’t want him. But forty-two days ago, Mydei tried to take Phainon aside during their last meeting, only to be brushed off immediately. As if Phainon thought Mydei couldn’t even handle rejection.

So upon arriving in Okhema for the Festival of Phagousa, he didn’t even try. He is the head of the Kremnoan Council. He can do far, far better than a man who won’t even look him in the eyes after promising him that Mydei was the only man he would ever love.

He was doing fairly well at ignoring Phainon’s existence entirely—that is, until Lady Hyacine asked him if he would pretty please help him unpack the new shipment of medical supplies she had acquired. He went to the room where she indicated they were—and then, right there, with an armful of bandages, is the man that’s been haunting him for the past three months.

“Oh!” Lady Hyacine says. “Phainon! Great—Althaea said she told you where the boxes were, but I was worried you’d get lost along the way. Her directions… aren’t exactly the clearest,” she says—going on and on about some new assistant of hers. Mydei is only half-listening—too preoccupied with glaring at the man before him. Hyacine pretends not to notice.

“Yeah, I—“ Phainon clears his throat. “I found it fine. Thanks.”

“Great,” Hyacine beams, clapping her hands. “I’m so glad to have you both here. It’ll go so much quicker with the both of you. Maybe you guys can even make a little competition out of it—just like old times, right? You guys haven’t had one of those in awhile.”

Mydei chokes on air. There’s no way Hyacine could’ve known it, but the last competition they had took the form of “who can make the other come the most.”

Clearly, Phainon is just as flustered by the memory—one of his wings flares out, and Mydei watches in slow motion as the pile of boxes clatters to the ground. Despite himself, a flare of satisfaction hisses in Mydei’s chest—it’s good to know that Phainon hasn’t completely forgotten about it. Fun to watch him panic, even for just a second.

Hyacine yelps. “Oh! Careful! I think there’s still probably some vaccines left in there.”

Mydei’s mirth dissipates immediately as he shoots Phainon another glare. If his people fall to a disease brought by the new interstellar travelers, he’ll never forgive the man. At least Phainon seems apologetic about it. At least he’s apologetic about something.

“I’ll be more careful in the future, Lady Hyacine,” he says, hands folded up in front of him like a child.

“Don’t worry about it, Lord Phainon,” Hyacine says, her smile slightly strained. “Anyway! Like I said, I need it all sorted. Don’t worry about bringing it back to the Garden of Life—right here is fine. Once we know what’s in each box, it’ll be much faster for my assistants to distribute it where it needs to go.”

“Understood,” Mydei says, crossing his arms over his chest. He gives Hyacine another stiff nod, watching as she turns away with a flounce.

Mydei glares up at Phainon, rage roaring through his veins like a wild beast. Somehow, the fact that he has to look so far up now makes this so much worse.

“Let’s just get this over with,” he mutters to himself, his spine rigid.

They work in silence for a few minutes, the silence a living thing. It shoulders between them, muscular and sleek, like the sea monsters that writhed around Mydei in the sea of souls. Mydei rips open the packaging—scans what’s inside. Sorts it. It takes every iota of control in him to keep his hands and gaze steady. He knows, thanks to the Trailblazer’s offhanded comment, that his Primum Mobile is restraint. Right now, it’s difficult to believe, given that his entire body is baying for blood. He only barely keeps his mouth shut.

Think about anything else. Pomegranate juice. Castorice’s poetry. Fresh honeycakes.

It works well enough. He’s internally drafting a response to Krateros’s latest letter when Phainon opens his mouth. Immediately, Mydei feels his control dangle by a thread.

Phainon clears his throat, dusting off his hands as he sets the last box onto the pile by the door. “Well, um. That’s everything. I guess we should…”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “Running away again?” he says dryly, brushing off his chlamys.

Phainon’s face twists. “I just—I’ve been busy.”

“Have you?” Mydei says coolly. “You must have been. You’ve barely even spared me a glance since you got here.”

Phainon’s whole body shudders at that—something too much like guilt shuddering across his face. He looks like a scolded child—wide eyes, bitten lips, trembling hands. All at once, the rage and grief that had been simmering in Mydei’s chest boils over—his whole body is aflame as he slams the last box down, the thud shuddering through the air.

“Mydei,” Phainon scolds weakly, his eyes glued to the box—but Mydei, Titans—no, Aeons—help him, isn’t even thinking about that thing.

“Phainon,” he retorts. “Are you going to deny it? Or are you going to flee like a beast?”

“Mydeimos—“

“It’s funny,” Mydei continues, his hands snapping into fists. “I once thought you were a brave man. Admirable. Loyal. Loving,” he spits, the words sizzling like poison. “The only man who could ever stand beside me as my equal. But now I know that you never thought—“

“Stop,” Phainon hisses—and several things happen at once.

Great wings tear from Phainon’s back—golden blood spraying onto marble. Obsidian sears its way up the curve of Phainon’s neck. The stupid gloves he’d been wearing split—Mydei can’t tell if they’re claws or gauntlets, but jagged edges burst from the fingers.

Mydei swallows hard—then allows his rage to set him alight.

“Oh,” he drawls. “So you’re threatening me, now. Make no mistake, Deliverer—I may not have the gaze of Nanook, but I’ve had nearly a thousand years to hone my skills in this timeline. I was your match then—and I’m your match now.”

Phainon’s eyes blaze—golden irises exploding out into the whites of his eyes. “Mydeimos—“

Mydei spreads his arms, chest heaving. “Are you going to fight me, Deliverer? Kill me?”

He doesn’t mean it—but for a moment—a fleeting, fleeting moment—he thinks Phainon might. His gaze goes steely. The whole room trembles—from the window, black and red erupt across the sky, casting the room in a bloody glow.

“Kill you?” he echoes dangerously. His voice is little more than a rasp—nails on a chalkboard, a sword screaming against a shield. Mydei, despite himself, can barely breathe. Phainon’s very gaze is something visceral—waves of heat blistering Mydei’s skin.

“Kill you?” he repeats hoarsely. “Mydeimos, I…” he laughs—low. Cruel. Agonized. “I am a beast. Nothing…. nothing better than a monster. I—I can’t deny it. But you, you—if I had a fraction of your honor, your bravery—I wouldn’t…” he grits his teeth. “I wouldn’t… I would’ve been better than this. But you… you are the thing that kept me sane. When my heart burned to ashes, when my ribs turned into dust, when my mind melted into glass—“ he laughs again—a hyena’s cry, hoarse and broken. “Mydeimos, when your blood was on my hands—“ his voice cracks, shattering into nothing.

When the next wave of heat hits, Mydei instinctively throws up his hands in front of his face, feeling the skin peel and blister. His mind reels—stumbling through countless memories that had left him baffled until now. There’s no way. But—

Then—all at once—the heat fades. The red light is swallowed up by the evening sun—when Mydei lowers his hands, the sun lazes out from behind a cloud. Phainon blinks—his eyes are back to the way they were, white and gold, the same as that infernal coat. Phainon’s wings still stir the stifling air, and his jaw is clenched. But the air is cooler—more like a bonfire than standing in the flames.

“I should go,” Phainon says stiffly. He stuffs his hands in his pockets—wicked claws nicking Aglaea’s impeccable needlework.

Mydei should let him go. He should. But instead—the word monster ringing in his ears like a battlecry—he says the first thing that comes to mind. There’s no way he’s right. But the phrasing was so similar. And if he is right—

“I could hear prayers,” he says abruptly. Tightening his grip on the railing.

“What?” Phainon chokes out.

“I assumed you didn’t know,” Mydei continues, staring out at the square—the marble of rebuilt statues winking where the city once stood in embers. “I doubt it’s something I ever would have had the reason or opportunity to tell you in any cycle. But it started immediately after I acquired Nikador’s Coreflame.”

“Prayers,” Phainon echoes weakly. “So you—“

“As long as they were conducted properly,” Mydei continues, the familiar prayer falling from his lips with the ease of breathing. “The Undefeated Overlord of the Battlefield, King of Castrum Kremnos and the Ruins, Grand Artisan of Chariots, the Throne of Corpses, Father of Victory, The Tyrant of Glories, lightning that shatters earth and seas, Guardian of Amphoreus, Strife Titan, Lance of Fury, Mydeimos.”

Mydei does not bother to look back at Phainon—but he knows with the certainty of Talanton that the man’s face is white as bone.

“I didn’t realize at first,” Mydei admits. “After all—no one addressed prayers to me until after the news of me accepting the Coreflame spread. But after it did… the first prayer I received was in the midst of a battle against a legion of Daemons. It was a young woman—in her twenties, perhaps. She prayed for bravery. She was preparing to embark on a mission outside of the Holy City.”

“I nearly dropped my spear,” he says wryly. “There I was—alone in the ruins of my homeland, and I heard the voice of a woman speaking in my mother tongue. Praying the words I had uttered myself a thousand times in my youth. Clear as if she were behind me. And from there… the prayers came in a flood. When I was wading through the Sea of Souls—wrestling to keep my mind and heart intact—I heard the voices of my people. The old. The young. Wishing me well. Begging for assistance. Blessings.”

“What happened?” Phainon croaks suddenly. “To the woman?”

Mydei casts a glance backward—his first since he had begun this line of discussion. Phainon looks winded—chest heaving, skin pale, fingers trembling. A man at the end of his rope. Mydei chooses mercy—as much as he can give it.

“She died,” he says bluntly, staring back out at the city. “But she thanked me for my sacrifice. In her death throes—she prayed I might bless her children with the bravery I had inspired in her.”

“Mydeimos…”

“The children are well,” Mydei says stiffly, his knuckles white beneath his gauntlets. “I checked on them when Amphoreus was reborn. Their father cares for them deeply. He thanked me for watching over his wife.”

Phainon goes silent—all that’s left between them is the rumblings of their people below.

“I heard every prayer,” Mydei continues, his gaze trained on the ruins of the Dawn Device. “Including the ones from you. I knew that you didn’t know I could hear them.” His lips quirk up. “You never would have been so honest otherwise.”

“I had no idea you could—that anyone—“

“I assumed not. Aglaea hardly had a need for prayers—her threads told her all she needed to know. And the Tribios were likely too fractured for prayers to reach them.”

Phainon is silent for a long moment. “The whole time, you—“

“I couldn’t respond to them,” Mydei admits. “All of my strength was used in subduing the Black Tide. But I heard them. That you were thinking of me—Titans, that you bothered to learn my peoples’ prayers, just to tell me about burned fish and tell me you hoped I wasn’t tripping over the ivy in Castrum Kremnos—“ he scoffs fondly.

“I was desperate for anything,” Phainon says hollowly. “To feel closer to you. So it—I just said anything. What I thought of dinner. When the baths were too hot. When I was—when I missed you. When I was worried about you.”

Mydei swallows hard. “I know.”

Silence lingers between them again. It’s nothing like it used to be—it’s crushing now, a pillar shattering the bones in Mydei’s chest.

“Your accent was horrible,” he finally says. A last-ditch attempt.

Phainon—finally—scoffs. Strangled. Shocked. Fond.

“Cut me some slack,” he says. “My teacher was gone.”

The silence is softer this time. Mydei even spares a glance at Phainon—his heart seizing at that familiar little smile playing on Phainon’s lips. Perhaps it’s because of that smile that he feels safe enough to say what he’s been trying to get at the whole time.

“I heard your prayers,” he repeats. “All of them.”

Phainon’s brow furrows. “What do you—“

“I didn’t know who it was,” Mydei says, glancing back at the view spilling out before them. “I hadn’t heard the Flame Reaver speak for long enough for me to put it together. And even if I had… I doubt I would have made the connection. Most of his prayers weren’t very long, anyway. Segmented. I doubt he could get much out, knowing what I do now.”

Phainon goes very still. Then the panic sets in. All in the eyes—like a man with a dagger to his throat. Phainon opens his mouth—but Mydei cuts him off.

“You prayed to me,” Mydei says. “Even knowing you had to kill me, you prayed to me. For bravery. For strength. For me.”

“Mydei, I—“

Mydei turns to him, his arms crossed. Eyebrow raised. Posture straight. “You tell me that you are a monster. But a truly evil man would not pray for my comfort. He would not pray for my safety. He would not wish to have ‘a fraction of my bravery’ even when his ‘heart burned to ash’ and ‘ribs crumbled to dust.’”

Mydei waits a moment, chest heaving. “He would not pray that he could make me proud.”

He’s still furious. He is. But for Phainon to say he’s a monster—Mydei can’t abide by that. Won’t abide by that.

“Phainon. Khaslana—“ and Mydei is not blind to the way the name makes Phainon shiver—“Don’t you dare misunderstand me. You are not a beast. You are not a monster. I’m—“ he sets his jaw. “I’m sorry that I said that. That’s not why I’m treating you like this. I’m furious because you lied.”

“You once swore to me forever,” Mydei seethes, stalking forward as Phainon stumbles back. “You swore to me your tomorrow. That if there were a day beyond this—beyond the fighting, beyond destruction, beyond death—beyond Chrysos Heirs and Coreflames—I would be yours, and you would be mine.”

“Mydei,” Phainon croaks.

Mydei spreads his arms—gestures to the remnants of the Dawn Device. To the real sun, beaming in the cloud-kissed sky. “If you regret it,” he forces out. “Say it. I won’t blame you. I won’t be angry. But it is that day, Deliverer. Will you make good on that promise?”

“Mydei, you don’t understand. The things I’ve done—you shouldn’t—“

And it is this statement that finally makes something in Mydei snap. He jerks Phainon forward by that damned collar, pulling him down to be eye-to-eye.

“You presume to know what’s best for me?” he snarls.

Phainon squeaks. And there is something very, very satisfying about making the man who burst from the body of a Lord Ravager shrink into himself like a mouse.

“Answer me. Because to me, the answer is very clear. You cannot even meet my eyes, Deliverer,” Mydei seethes, the metal of his gauntlets creaking. “Or did my confession mean nothing to you? Was it a mere careless comment in the throes of passion? Is loving me—“ and Mydei’s voice does not break, it does not—“is loving me so undesirable that you wish to undo it?”

“No! No,” Phainon blurts out, his eyes ablaze and his hands trembling as they dart up over Mydei’s. “No, Mydei, I promise,” he vows, his voice low and fervent as the flames ripping through forests in Dawnmaker’s wake. “I promise. It’s not—it’s not that. You’re—fuck, you’re perfect. It’s just—“
